k1p1-2.name: text#2
k1p1-2.text: KP03 What a zero gradient means

k1p1-6.name: text#6
k1p1-6.text:
no direction goes lower
the first-order change is zero in every direction

k1p1-11.name: text#11
k1p1-11.text: direction: local minimum $\Rightarrow$ zero gradient, not the other way round. A necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

k1p1-15.name: text#15
k1p1-15.text: in code the gradient is never exactly zero: use a small threshold $\varepsilon$

k1p2-14.name: text#14
k1p2-14.text: can one more step still lower it?

k1p2-27.name: text#27
k1p2-27.text: the first three watch training itself

k1p2-31.name: text#31
k1p2-31.text: deep learning often uses the last two: full gradients are costly and SGD gradients are noisy

k1p3-2.name: text#2
k1p3-2.text: On one path, the criteria stop in different places

k1p3-41.name: text#41
k1p3-41.text: on the same path the two rules differ by 35 steps

k1p3-43.name: text#43
k1p3-43.text: the loss-change rule stops early: the gradient is still over 8 times the threshold

k1p4-15.name: text#15
k1p4-15.text: with a gradient norm of $1.66$ the loss change is already only $0.16$: “barely falling” is not “flat”

k1p4-17.name: text#17
k1p4-17.text: the loss change is of the order of the squared gradient norm (KP02's first-order estimate)

k1p5-2.name: text#2
k1p5-2.text: Looks like time to stop, but it is not

k1p5-24.name: text#24
k1p5-24.text:
at the origin the gradient norm is $0$ and any gradient rule declares arrival
yet it is not a minimum: high-dimensional non-convex surfaces are full of saddles

k1p5-27.name: text#27
k1p5-27.text:
saturated regions or wide plains: the loss falls by only $0.00001$ for many steps
stopping early on the loss change may miss a steep descent ahead

k1p5-29.name: text#29
k1p5-29.text: the gradient norm alone is fooled by saddles; the loss change alone by plateaus

k1p6-2.name: text#2
k1p6-2.text: What to do: never bet on one indicator

k1p6-6.name: text#6
k1p6-6.text:
small gradient norm,
and loss change small for $N$ steps,
or step length $\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|\le\varepsilon_w$

k1p6-9.name: text#9
k1p6-9.text:
whatever happens,
stop at $K_{\max}$,
never endless

k1p6-12.name: text#12

k1p6-14.name: text#14
k1p6-14.text: “training convergence is bad” is too blunt: low training loss does not guarantee generalization, hence the validation loss

k1p6-16.name: text#16
k1p6-16.text: “where to stop” is not purely a mathematical question

k1p7-2.name: text#2
k1p7-2.text: Last: myths and the next question

k1p7-6.name: text#6
k1p7-6.text: saddles and plateaus can have small gradients too

k1p7-9.name: text#9
k1p7-9.text: the loss change is of squared order and can be far smaller

k1p7-11.name: text#11
k1p7-11.text: “the lower the training loss the better”

k1p7-12.name: text#12
k1p7-12.text: watch the validation loss or you may overfit

k1p7-14.name: text#14
k1p7-14.text: Before stopping: can the step size of each step be chosen automatically and safely?

steps.label: KP03 What a zero gradient means
Zero gradient · 1/7
steps.speakerNotes: Suppose the loss is differentiable and w star is a local minimum. No direction goes lower there, so the first-order change is zero in every direction.

steps.label: Zero gradient · 1/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first-order optimality condition: the gradient is zero. A point with zero gradient is a stationary point.

steps.label: Zero gradient · 1/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Note the direction: a local minimum implies zero gradient, not the other way round. Zero gradient is necessary, not sufficient.

steps.label: Zero gradient · 1/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: In code we can only set a small threshold and stop when the gradient length falls below it.

steps.label: Zero gradient · 1/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: \|\nabla f(w^{(k+1)})\|_2\le\varepsilon in code the gradient is never exactly zero: use a small threshold \varepsilon

steps.label: Five indicators · 2/7
steps.speakerNotes: The gradient norm is only one. The first three watch training itself: is the slope flat, can another step lower the loss, has the direction stabilized.

steps.label: Five indicators · 2/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The fourth watches resources: the iteration budget, has the compute run out.

steps.label: Five indicators · 2/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The fifth watches generalization: validation loss stops improving, would more training overfit. Deep learning often uses the last two because full-training-set gradients are costly and SGD gradients are noisy, never exactly zero.

steps.label: Five indicators · 2/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: validation loss validation loss stops improving would more training overfit? the fifth watches generalization deep learning often uses the last two: full gradients are costly and SGD gradients are noisy

steps.label: One path · 3/7
steps.speakerNotes: On KP01's toy bowl with learning rate 0.06, look at the gradient norm and loss change at each step.

steps.label: One path · 3/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Take threshold 0.2. The loss-change rule triggers at step 29, when the gradient norm is still 1.662, over eight times the threshold, and the loss 1.38 is still far from the minimum.

steps.label: One path · 3/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The gradient-norm rule only triggers at step 64, when the loss is 0.0182.

steps.label: One path · 3/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: On the same path the two criteria differ by 35 steps.

steps.label: One path · 3/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: on the same path the two rules differ by 35 steps the loss-change rule stops early: the gradient is still over 8 times the threshold

steps.label: The square · 4/7
steps.speakerNotes: Why the disagreement? The loss change is about the learning rate times the squared gradient norm.

steps.label: The square · 4/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The gradient norm is first power.

steps.label: The square · 4/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The former is the square of the latter times the learning rate. At step 29: 0.06 times 1.662 squared, about 0.166, close to 0.161.

steps.label: The square · 4/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: So with a gradient norm of 1.66 the loss change is already only 0.16. Barely falling does not mean flat.

steps.label: The square · 4/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: with a gradient norm of 1.66 the loss change is already only 0.16: “barely falling” is not “flat” the loss change is of the order of the squared gradient norm (KP02's first-order estimate)

steps.label: Saddles and plateaus · 5/7
steps.speakerNotes: A saddle: take x squared minus y squared; the gradient at the origin is zero and a gradient rule declares arrival at once. But it rises along x and falls along y, so the origin is a saddle, not a minimum.

steps.label: Saddles and plateaus · 5/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Plateaus: in saturated regions or wide plains the surface is very flat and the loss falls by only a hundred-thousandth for many steps. Stopping early on the loss change leaves the model halfway.

steps.label: Saddles and plateaus · 5/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: plateau saturated regions or wide plains: the loss falls by only 0.00001 for many steps stopping early on the loss change may miss a steep descent ahead the gradient norm alone is fooled by saddles; the loss change alone by plateaus

steps.label: Use them together · 6/7
steps.speakerNotes: In practice never bet on a single indicator.

steps.label: Use them together · 6/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: First, combine rules: a small gradient and a loss change that stays small for many steps, or a small step length.

steps.label: Use them together · 6/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Second, a budget: whatever happens, stop at the maximum number of steps.

steps.label: Use them together · 6/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Third, early stopping on validation loss: deep learning does not push training loss to zero; measure the validation loss now and then and stop when it stops improving.

steps.label: Use them together · 6/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Saying training convergence is bad is too blunt. More precisely, lower training loss does not guarantee good generalization, so we need the validation loss.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7
steps.speakerNotes: Finally, the common myths and the question left for the next unit.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: “a small gradient means a minimum”. saddles and plateaus can have small gradients too

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: “no more loss decrease means convergence”. the loss change is of squared order and can be far smaller

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: “the lower the training loss the better”. watch the validation loss or you may overfit

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Before stopping: can the step size of each step be chosen automatically and safely?
